extracted.intended_audience: linguists, media researchers, journalism students and practising journalists
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and analytic criteria for studying and producing the language of news media, including sampling decisions, production roles, editing operations, audience design, news values and the formal structure of news stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasons to study media language
rubrics_metrics.description: Seven motivations listed for studying media language: 1) Accessibility of media as a source of data for some language feature we want to study; 2) Interest in the way the media use some language feature, also found in ordinary speech; 3) Interest in media’s role in affecting language in wider society; 4) Interest in what media language reveals as a mirror of the wider society and culture; 5) Interest in how media language affects attitudes and opinions in society through the way it presents people and issues; 6) Availability, media language is easier to collect than conversation; 7) There’s no Observer’s Paradox since media language is already intended for mass public consumption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these motivations to justify corpus selection and research questions; emphasizes both practical access and theoretical interest (effects on society, reflection of culture).

rubrics_metrics.name: Universe and sample decisions for media corpora
rubrics_metrics.description: Decisions on gathering a corpus of media language are required in three main areas: (1) The genres (particular kind of media content of interest — e.g. news, classified advertising, game shows, weather forecasts); (2) The media outlets (the publications, television channels or radio stations which carry the content); (3) 'Outputs' (what the media outlets produce — specific newscasts, advertisements or programmes — and the time period to be covered).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit about genre, outlet and time-window choices; samples can range from single clips to months of broadcast or stories from many countries. Tailor sampling to the analytic variable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defining genres and editorial categories
rubrics_metrics.description: In a newspaper, everything other than advertising is called 'editorial' and includes written copy (news, hard news, headlines, feature articles), service information, opinion (editorials, columns, letters, reviews) and special-topic news (sports, racing, arts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish hard news vs features (hard news = reports of recent events; features = longer background/interpretive pieces often bylined). Note fuzzy boundaries; classify samples accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hard news vs feature (soft) distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: Newsworker’s basic distinction is between hard news and features. Hard news: reports of accidents, crimes, announcements and other events occurring since the previous issue — the place where a distinctive news style is found. Features (soft news): longer articles providing background, sometimes 'editorialize', usually bylined; more liberty of style and often written by non-journalists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect different linguistic conventions and levels of authorial freedom in hard vs soft news; treat them as separate analytic categories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Where news copy comes from (origins and recycling)
rubrics_metrics.description: Most news outlets carry far more news originated by other organizations than by their own journalists. International news largely derives from the 'Big Four' agencies (Reuters, AP, UPI, AFP); domestic non-local news often from internal agencies; much local-seeming copy often originates from press offices. A large proportion of news is recycled talk about talk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing style/origin, account for agency-originated copy and press-office text as distinct inputs; trace provenance because editing practices differ by source.

rubrics_metrics.name: Researcher approach to media organizations ('porcupine reaction')
rubrics_metrics.description: Media personnel often have a 'porcupine reaction'—a nervous reaction to criticism—that can jeopardize research. The likelihood of reaction should not deter researchers but should forewarn them to approach media organizations and present research with care.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan ethics/approach and stakeholder communication; anticipate institutional defensiveness when requesting access or publishing findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Roles in producing news language (Hymes/Goffman/Bell mapping)
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiple roles contribute to news language: Principal (proprietor, managers), Author (journalist generates news language), Editor (overseer, copy editor, interpreter responsible for prominence and presentation), Animator/Transmitter (newsreader, typesetter, proofreader responsible for accurate transmission), Technician (printers, camera operators with no language input).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Map the production chain in your study outlet to identify who can modify language at each stage; treat authorship as distributed rather than solely bylined.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorship in journalism (journalists as compilers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists are authors in occupation but often act as compilers rather than sole originators — embedding existing text and using pre-fabricated written sources; a byline is no guarantee of sole authorship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume byline = original composition; analyze embedding, reuse and source reproduction practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editing operations and their effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Editing commonly involves (a) Information deletions (most common operation), (b) Lexical substitutions (replace words), (c) Syntactic editing rules; editing transforms a text into another text different in form but congruent in meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When comparing versions, look for deletion, substitution and syntactic restructuring; deletions can preserve grammaticality while altering emphasis or content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Four functions for copy editing
rubrics_metrics.description: Copy editing serves four functions: Cutting (delete real/redundant information), Clarifying, Maximize news value (choosing alternative lead, reordering), Standardizing language (apply house style: syntax, lexicon, spelling & pronunciation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess edits by which function they perform; use these categories to code editorial interventions and to understand stylistic normalization.

rubrics_metrics.name: General guidelines on writing news (lead and order)
rubrics_metrics.description: Lead and order are the most important aspects of maximizing news value; the lead paragraph functions as the primary abstract/summary and carries evaluation to focus the story. House styles and agency texts provide normative guidance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate stories on whether lead provides required 'who, what, when, where' orientation and an evaluative focus; expect subeditors to rewrite for lead and order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience characteristics of mass communication
rubrics_metrics.description: Six characteristics: large audience; public accessibility; heterogeneity of audience; simultaneous contact with widely separated individuals; one-directional flow and impersonality; the mass audience as a creation of modern society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these characteristics to frame hypotheses about style choices (e.g., generalization, clarity, impersonality) in mass-mediated texts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience roles (addressee, auditor, overhearer, eavesdropper)
rubrics_metrics.description: Audience members occupy graded roles: Addressee (known & addressed), Auditor (present but not directly addressed), Overhearer (speaker knows they are there), Eavesdropper (presence not known). Mass communication places many audience members toward peripheral roles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish intended addressed audience from peripheral/latent audiences when analyzing style and indexing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience design (responsive vs initiative style shifts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Style variation can be explained by audience design: intra-speaker variation correlates with attributes of hearers. Speakers sometimes respond to their audience (responsive) and sometimes take initiative to redefine relationships (initiative). More formal genres (newscasting) are responsive; advertising/on-air discussions are more initiative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model stylistic variation in terms of audience design; predict where responsive or initiative shifts are likely across genres.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accommodation theory and audience accommodation
rubrics_metrics.description: Speakers accommodate speech style to their hearers (approval-seeking, clarity). In mass media, communicators aim to win audience approval and ensure signal clarity. If communicators fail to accommodate, audiences may self-select to those matching the style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use accommodation as a mechanism to explain convergence/divergence of style and audience composition; expect station-level 'targets'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stylistic variable as audience-status diagnostic (determiner deletion)
rubrics_metrics.description: A rule characteristic of news language is deletion of determiners in appositional naming expressions (e.g., [the] Australian entrepreneur Alan Bond). Determiner deletion rates correlate with readership social status: 'popular' papers delete more; 'quality' papers delete fewer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use measurable linguistic variables (like determiner deletion) as diagnostics of audience profile and station/newspaper style; compare across outlets and time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editing-for-style rules (copy editors reinsert determiners)
rubrics_metrics.description: Copy editors shift incoming copy towards station targets; they never apply a rule to delete determiners from incoming copy, but reinsert determiners because their station target is lower deletion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When tracing stylistic change across versions, expect systematic editorial moves intended to align external input to internal style norms; coding should track direction of change (insert vs delete).

rubrics_metrics.name: Referee design (initiative shifts toward a third-party model)
rubrics_metrics.description: Referee design: speakers diverge away from addressee-appropriate style towards that of a third party (a referee) — ingroup vs outgroup referees, short-term vs long-term; outgroup referee design may be long-term or institutionalized (diglossia).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify whether style choices invoke a reference model (British vs American news norms, prestige varieties); treat referee effects as rhetorical/identity strategies rather than audience response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advertisements as initiative genre
rubrics_metrics.description: Advertisements function initiative-ly — to persuade, challenge, seize attention, tell an anecdote — employing creative language (including foreign languages/non-native dialects) and simulating distance/intimacy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect high linguistic creativity and deliberate departures from audience-tailored norms in advertising; analyze ads separately from news for rhetorical strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: News story as story (structure and genre-specific narrative functions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists write stories (not merely articles); a story has structure, direction, point and viewpoint. Key narrative components: Lead (primary abstract/evaluation), Headline (abstract of abstract), Orientation (who, when, where), Evaluation (establish significance), Resolution (often in lead not end), Coda generally absent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate news texts on presence and quality of lead, headline, orientation and evaluative focus; distinguish news schemata from personal narrative schemata.

rubrics_metrics.name: News values (factors determining newsworthiness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Lists of news values: in actors/events (negativity, recency, proximity, consonance, unambiguity, unexpectedness/novelty, superlativeness, relevance, personalization, eliteness, attribution, facticity); in the news process (continuity, competition, co-option, composition, predictability, prefabrication); in the news text (clarity, brevity, colour). Galtung & Ruge principles: news factors are cumulative and can compensate for each other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these factors to assess/select stories and to code editorial decisions; consider cumulative scoring and compensatory interactions among factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Macrorules for summarizing news discourse
rubrics_metrics.description: Van Dijk’s macrorules reduce discourse to kernel information via three operations: Deletion of information, Generalization, and 'Construction' (selection/combination that produces macropropositions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply macrorules to model how journalists condense multi-topic discourse into a focused news story; code transformations from source to published text using these operations.

rubrics_metrics.name: News schemata and formal categories of news texts
rubrics_metrics.description: News schemata are the formal categories into which news can be analysed (e.g., Abstract, Headline, Lead, Attribution, Place, Source, Time, Events/Episodes, Actors, Action, Setting, Follow-up, Background, Reaction, History, Consequences, Evaluation, Expectations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the provided structural model of news texts to segment and annotate stories; expect embedded episodes and multiple macropropositions; map headline/lead to extracted components.
